.

.

body_text:
🇳🇱Ekster เป็นแบรนด์ ทำ Cardholder แบบพรีเมี่ยม จากประเทศเนเธอร์แลนด์  ตอนที่เอาเข้ามา เห็นราคาต้นทุนรวมแล้ว ผมก็ยังกังวลว่ามันจะขายได้มั้ย ในคลาดที่มี cardholder ไม่มีแบรนด์ขายอันละไม่กี่ร้อย
.
👍สุดท้าย ของดีมีคุณภาพ มันก็ขายตัวมันเองได้ ถึงแม้มันไม่ได้ขายดีมากอะไร แต่ก็ถือว่าขายได้ดีเกินความคาดหวังของผมไปเยอะ   
.
💳EKSTER cardholder คือกล่องเก็บบัตรเดรดิตดีไซน์ดี มี RFID block ออกแบบปุ่มกดที่ไม่เหมือนใคร ให้สามารถกดได้หลากหลายทาง สามารถกดปุ่ม ด้วยการบีบมือให้อุ้งมือกดปุ่มแทนการใช้นิ้วกดได้  ทำให้มันใช้สะดวกขึ้น  และที่ไม่สามารถอธิบายได้ คือ ตัวปุ่มกด มันให้ฟีลลิ่งในการกดและเด้ง ที่ดีมากๆ
.
🤔รุ่นใหม่ออกมา Ekster Cardholder Pro ตอนมาถึง แว่บแรก ผมยังงงว่ามันต่างจากรุ่นเดิมตรงไหน  แต่ผมเอามาเทียบกัน  จะเห็นชัดว่าตัวกล่องหนาขึ้นเล็กน้อยสามารถใส่บัตรได้มากขึ้น 1 ใบ รวมเป็นใส่บัตรได้ 5-7 ใบ ขึ้นอยู่กับความหนาของบัตร   
.
🫶อีกจุดที่แตกต่างชัดเจน คือ ปรับมุมโค้งขอบด้านล่างและปรับปุ่มกดให้เรียบคลีนขึ้น กลายเป็นการปรับน้อย แต่ดูดี ลงตัวขึ้นมาก
.
😀วัสดุ พรีเมี่ยม เป็น อลูมิเนียม 6061 space grade และ มีแบบ carbon fiber ด้วย
.
😀อีกหนึ่งเอกลักษณ์ที่คงเดิมคือ สายรัดกระเป๋าที่มาพร้อม back plate ใช้ใส่บัตรเสริม หรือแบงค์ได้ และยังมี accessory อีกหลายอย่างให้หามาใช้
.
💶จริงๆ ราคาตามหน้าเว็บมันแพงขึ้นไปกว่ารุ่นเดิม แต่ผมให้คงราคาขาย เท่ารุ่นเดิมเลย เพราะอยากให้ซื้อหากันได้ไม่ยากเกินไป
.
🔖Ekster cardholder Pro (Aluminium)
ราคา 3,950 บาท
Shopee https://s.shopee.co.th/8Kc4FV8zwq
Lazada https://s.lazada.co.th/s.EbTZz?cc
--------------------------------
🔖Ekster cardholder Pro  (Carbon)
ราคา 4.950 บาท
Shopee https://s.shopee.co.th/4filsnrI5V
Lazada https://s.lazada.co.th/s.Ebgyl?cc
--------------------------------

Carry more. Settle for less? Never.

The UTC x Secrid XI Anniversary Twinwallet is designed for those who refuse to compromise.

Double the patented Cardprotectors mean room for up to 16 cards. A dedicated billfold and extra compartments keep cash, receipts, and business cards organized. The exclusive gold Premium Collection lever delivers Secrid’s iconic click with every use, while Black Crisple leather and UTC’s signature orange interior complete a wallet that’s as refined as it is functional.

“Secrid has never simply been another brand in our stores. We’ve grown together over the last eleven years, built on the same belief that thoughtful design, responsible manufacturing, and products made to last will always stand the test of time. " Hans Fernandez, Chief Curator, UTC.

Built for everyday carry. Created to celebrate 11 years.

Available exclusively at Urban Traveller & Co. Read more https://bit.ly/4wOeeGW 

#UTC11Years #UTCxSecrid #CarryEveryMoment #Secrid #EverydayCarry

body_text:
Your wallet is a walking target. 📡💳

Thieves don't need to pick your pocket anymore—they just need a scanner. But bulky wallets with cheap RFID sleeves? They ruin your suit line and still leave you guessing.

Meet the RFID Blocking Metal Card Holder—ultra-slim, military-grade stainless steel armor for your cards. Designed for men who want security without the bulk, this pocket-sized vault slips into your front pocket like it was never there. 🛡️✨

Why it belongs in your pocket:
🔒 Advanced RFID Blocking – blocks 13.56 MHz signals from skimmers, protecting your credit cards, debit cards, and ID from wireless theft.
📏 Ultra-Slim & Pocket-Friendly – holds 6–8 cards in a profile thinner than most phones, yet slides out effortlessly.
🛠️ Heavy-Duty Stainless Steel – built to survive drops, scratches, and years of daily carry; won't warp or crack like plastic.
💼 Business-Ready Design – sleek brushed metal finish that pairs perfectly with a suit, briefcase, or travel bag.

From boardrooms to airport lounges, keep your financial data locked down and your style on point.

🛒 Tap to get yours and carry smarter, safer, and sharper. 👇

Small enough to take everywhere. Roomy enough that you don’t have to edit your life down to three cards.

Go ahead. Give your overstuffed wallet a well-earned retirement. Shop the Lo now.

cards.body:
At 61, my daughter found every account, policy and password we own in nineteen minutes.

Without one phone call to a helpline.

Here is what I did.

If you are a woman over 55 and you are the one who quietly keeps this family running, the one who knows which account the private health cover comes out of and where the spare key lives, I want to tell you about the conversation I wish someone had sat me down for three years ago.

It would have saved me a year of low-level dread, one of the hardest afternoons of my life in a solicitor's office, and the money I wasted on things that did absolutely nothing.

I am writing this because last month, at 61, I sat at my kitchen table and watched my youngest daughter find every account, every policy and every password we own in nineteen minutes.

Without ringing anyone.

Without asking me once.

And the thing that finally made it possible was almost the opposite of what everyone had been telling me to do for years.

My name is Carol.

I am 61.

I live just outside Bendigo.

Two grown daughters, one grandson who rates my roast potatoes far higher than my baking.

I ran the office of a secondary school for twenty-nine years before I retired.

Nothing in that building moved without me knowing where it was.

Which is exactly why what happened between 58 and 60 rattled me.

Before I tell you what I did about it, I need to tell you the part that matters.

Because it changes what the fix actually has to be.

Three years ago I would have told you we were sorted.

Mirror wills, done properly in 2019.

A box file in the bureau labelled Important.

Sensible, boring arrangements.

The kind you tick off and stop thinking about.

Then my aunt June passed away at 87, and I was her executor.

June had a will.

June had a box file too.

It still took eleven weeks to get her first account released.

The official pages.

Retired deceased estate specialist.

It does not tell anyone what exists, where it is kept, or the order in which nineteen different organisations need to hear the news, each with its own clock.

The window before the paperwork machine starts — securing the house and mail, finding the original will, engaging the funeral director who registers the death, ordering enough certified certificates.

Roughly twenty-eight days.

The notifications.

The bank, the insurers, the super funds, each a separate call, in the right order or the wrong one.

Six months.

The window where everything is in motion — probate filing with the Supreme Court, the final ATO return, the super death benefit still working its way through the fund.

Not a thicker will.

Not a safe.

Not an app.

A handover file, he said.

Built in the order of the actual process, not the order of a stationery catalogue.

The plan on top.

The records underneath, feeding it.

I went home and spent two evenings checking him against the government's own sites.

Not glossy websites.

The official pages.

He was right.

The forty-eight hour window before the paperwork starts is real.

Services Australia really does stop at its own three services.

The super death benefit really can take months, sometimes years.

It is all there, once you know to look.

Two grown daughters, one grandson who rates my roast potatoes far higher than my baking.

I ran the office of a secondary school for twenty-nine years before I retired.

Nothing in that building moved without me knowing where it was.

Which is exactly why what happened between 58 and 60 rattled me.

Before I tell you what I did about it, I need to tell you the part that matters.

Because it changes what the fix actually has to be.

Three years ago I would have told you we were sorted.

Mirror wills, done properly in 2019.

A box file in the bureau labelled Important.

Sensible, boring arrangements.

The kind you tick off and stop thinking about.

Then my aunt June passed away at 87, and I was her executor.

June had a will.

June had a box file too.

It still took eleven weeks to get her first account released.

I counted, in the end, forty-one phone calls, most of them spent explaining the same sad news to a different call centre.

Her funeral sat on my credit card for four months.

And a small policy only surfaced eleven months later, in a bank statement nobody had known to look for.

At our last meeting, her solicitor was very kind about it.

He said most families arrive at his desk exactly the way we did.

He also said that when families hand the whole thing over to a firm instead, the bills typically start high and climb from there.

On the drive home, my eldest said the sentence I have not been able to un-hear since.

I gave myself six months to make sure it was not.

I booked us in and had the wills reviewed.

A few hundred dollars, and worth it, but twenty minutes of that meeting confirmed the wills were fine and always had been.

I bought a pack of plastic wallets and rebuilt the Important box.

I typed our accounts into a spreadsheet.

I wrote the girls a letter about where everything was and put it in the bureau.

I told David, my husband, that everything was in the box, and he nodded the way husbands do.

Five months in, I ran a little test.

Sunday lunch, as casual as I could make it.

I asked David to find our home insurance and tell me when it renewed.

He found the box.

He found three statements from three different years and could not tell which was current.

He did not know which account the private health cover came out of.

The password list was two years stale.

Twenty-five minutes in, he gave up and made a pot of tea.

Five months of genuine effort, and the box was still a scavenger hunt with a nicer label.

I was also noticing other things that bothered me.

The half past three accounting.

Lying awake, running through the list of what the girls would not know to look for.

The small jolt every time a renewal letter arrived from a company I had half forgotten we used.

I had always assumed that low hum was just part of being the organised one at 60.

It was not.

The shift for me came from an unexpected place.

A man named Ross Marsden gave a talk at a U3A meeting my neighbour Jean dragged me along to in October.

Retired deceased estate specialist.

Thirty-five years of it.

What it turned into was forty minutes on something I had never once heard explained properly.

He said the document families put their faith in, the will, is not the thing their children struggle with.

A will decides who inherits.

It does not tell anyone what exists, where it is kept, or the order in which nineteen different organisations need to hear the news, each with its own clock.

The struggle, he said, lives in the sequence.

And in Australia the sequence has a shape.

Forty-eight hours.

The window before the paperwork machine starts — securing the house and mail, finding the original will, engaging the funeral director who registers the death, ordering enough certified certificates.

Roughly twenty-eight days.

The notifications.

Services Australia has to be told within them if a payment was coming in — one call updates Centrelink, Medicare and Child Support, nothing else.

The bank, the insurers, the super funds, each a separate call, in the right order or the wrong one.

Six months.

The window where everything is in motion — probate filing with the Supreme Court, the final ATO return, the super death benefit still working its way through the fund.

Then he said the thing that made me write a note in my phone.

"The families who cope are not the ones with the best wills.

They are the ones where somebody left a sequence to follow.

There is one thing I told my own children to expect from me, and it is not what any of you think it is."

Not a thicker will.

Not a safe.

Not an app.

A handover file, he said.

Built in the order of the actual process, not the order of a stationery catalogue.

The plan on top.

The records underneath, feeding it.

I went home and spent two evenings checking him against the government's own sites.

Not glossy websites.

The official pages.

He was right.

The forty-eight hour window before the paperwork starts is real.

Services Australia really does stop at its own three services.

The super death benefit really can take months, sometimes years.

It is all there, once you know to look.

So of course my first move was to order the cheapest thing online that looked the part.

A $19.99 journal with a linen cover, one of those "when I am gone" memory books.

I filled in about a third of it over six weeks.

The chapters were alphabetical categories, not steps.

Half of it was American, with a page for social security and something called a 401k.

There was nowhere for the order of who to ring.

No deadlines.

No mention of probate or Services Australia anywhere in it.

I was essentially paying for nicer stationery.

It went in the drawer with the plastic wallets.

It had to be built on the real Australian sequence.

The funeral director and Births, Deaths and Marriages, Services Australia and everything it misses, probate, the ATO, the actual deadlines.

It had to hold the records that feed the plan.

Prompts for the exact reference numbers and documents each organisation asks for, not blank pages and good intentions.

And it had to be printable and physical.

One folder, on one shelf, that a person having the worst week of their life could follow page by page while a cup of tea goes cold beside them.

I came across The Aussie Estate Kit through a thread in a Facebook group for over-60s.

A woman had posted photographs of her finished folder, and underneath them, the message her son sent after she showed him.

The comments were genuine.

Other women posting theirs, arguing about which pack to choose, the usual.

Their Family Handover Kit is built around exactly the shape Ross described.

They call it 48-28-6.

A Start Here card with the first actions in order.

A checklist for each stage.

A register for every account, super and policy.

Ready to send letters for all the organisations that one call to Services Australia skips.

Written for Australia, in plain English, printed at home the same evening.

Every requirement I had written down, they had already addressed.

👉 This is the kit, if you want to look while you read (from $49):

https://theestatekit.com/au/nineteen-minutes

I ordered it on the Thursday.

I did not tell David.

I did not tell the girls.

I wanted to do it quietly, at my own pace, without anyone else's opinion in the room.

It took me two Sunday afternoons at the kitchen table.

The prompts tell you what goes where, so there was none of the blank page dread the journal gave me.

The first thing I noticed was not the folder.

It was half past three in the morning.

About nine days in, I realised I had stopped waking to run the list.

The accounting had gone quiet.

I was sleeping through to six, the way I used to.

Jean noticed before David did.

She said I seemed lighter on our Tuesday walk, and I could not immediately explain why.

At the six week mark I ran my test again, because I could not wait any longer.

Sunday lunch.

I put the folder on the table in front of my youngest, Becky, and set her a challenge.

The private health cover.

Dad's super.

The deeds.

The life policy, and who it names.

Nineteen minutes.

No phone calls.

She found the lot, including two things I would have struggled to lay hands on a year earlier.

She went quiet at the end, which is not like her.

Then she said,

"Mum, this might be the kindest thing you have ever done for us."

In the flurry of it, I pulled his page and had his Medicare number, his medications and his policy details at the front desk in under a minute, with my hands shaking.

That is when I understood the folder was never for some far off day.

It is for any Tuesday.

In May we had the wills looked over again, the scheduled visit.

I brought the folder along, mostly to ask where it ought to live.

I watched our solicitor leaf through it for a full two minutes.

He read the Start Here card twice.

Then he asked me where it was from, and wrote the name on his pad.

"I wish every client walked in with one of these," he said.

"Keep it with the will.

Not instead of it.

With it."

The folder is what your family will actually hold in their hands during the weeks the will cannot help them.

A spreadsheet only you understand is not.

Three months.

The registration and the notifications. Registering the death is free, but there is no single service that notifies everyone for you. The bank, Revenue, the DSP and its separate sections, each insurer, each one told one by one.

I am 61.

I ran the office of a secondary school for twenty-nine years before I retired.

The password list was two years stale.

Twenty-five minutes in, he gave up and made a pot of tea.

The half past three accounting.

Lying awake, running through the list of what the girls would not know to look for.

The small jolt every time a renewal letter arrived from a company I had half forgotten we used.

The struggle, he said, lives in the sequence.

Five days.

The legal window to register, order enough certificates, locate the will, establish who is acting, arrange the farewell.

The notifications.

Six months.

The deadline that catches everyone out.

Then he said the thing that made me write a note in my phone.

"The families who cope are not the ones with the best wills.

They are the ones where somebody left a sequence to follow.

Not a thicker will.

Not a safe.

Not an app.

A handover file, he said.

Built in the order of the actual process, not the order of a stationery catalogue.

The plan on top.

The records underneath, feeding it.

I went home and spent two evenings checking him against GOV.UK.

Not glossy websites.

The official pages.

He was right.

The five day registration window is real.

Tell Us Once really does stop at government departments.

The Inheritance Tax deadline really is the end of the sixth month.

It is all there, once you know to look.

It was half past three in the morning.

Sunday lunch.

I typed our accounts into a spreadsheet.

I wrote the girls a letter about where everything was and put it in the bureau.

I told David, my husband, that everything was in the box, and he nodded the way husbands do.

Sunday lunch, as casual as I could make it.

He found three statements from three different years and could not tell which was current.

He did not know which account the boiler cover came out of.

The password list was two years stale.

Twenty-five minutes in, he gave up and made a pot of tea.

Five months of genuine effort, and the box was still a scavenger hunt with a nicer label.

Lying awake, running through the list of what the girls would not know to look for.

The small jolt every time a renewal letter arrived from a company I had half forgotten we used.

I had always assumed that low hum was just part of being the organised one at 60.

It was not.

Retired probate practitioner.

Thirty-five years of it.

What it turned into was forty minutes on something I had never once heard explained properly.

He said the document families put their faith in, the will, is not the thing their children struggle with.

A will decides who inherits.

It does not tell anyone what exists, where it is kept, or the order in which nineteen different organisations need to hear the news, each with its own clock.

The struggle, he said, lives in the sequence.

And in England and Wales the sequence has a shape.

Five days.

The legal window to register, order enough certificates, locate the will, establish who is acting, arrange the farewell.

Roughly twenty-eight days.

The notifications.

Tell Us Once covers government departments and nothing else.

The bank, the mortgage, the insurers, the utilities, the private and workplace pensions, every one of those is a separate call, made in the right order or the wrong one.

Six months.

The deadline that catches everyone out.

Inheritance Tax is due by the end of the sixth month, and that clock does not pause while a family hunts for paperwork.

Then he said the thing that made me write a note in my phone.

"The families who cope are not the ones with the best wills.

They are the ones where somebody left a sequence to follow.

There is one thing I told my own children to expect from me, and it is not what any of you think it is."

Not a thicker will.

Not a safe.

Not an app.

A handover file, he said.

Built in the order of the actual process, not the order of a stationery catalogue.

The plan on top.

The records underneath, feeding it.

I went home and spent two evenings checking him against GOV.UK.

Not glossy websites.

The official pages.

He was right.

The five day registration window is real.

Tell Us Once really does stop at government departments.

The Inheritance Tax deadline really is the end of the sixth month.

It is all there, once you know to look.

The chapters were alphabetical categories, not steps.

Half of it was American, with a page for social security and something called a 401k.

There was nowhere for the order of who to ring.

No deadlines.

No mention of probate or Tell Us Once anywhere in it.

I was essentially paying for nicer stationery.

It went in the drawer with the plastic wallets.

I went back to what Robert had actually described and wrote myself three requirements.

It had to be built on the real England and Wales sequence.

The registrar, Tell Us Once and everything it misses, probate, HMRC, the actual deadlines.

It had to hold the records that feed the plan.

Prompts for the exact reference numbers and documents each organisation asks for, not blank pages and good intentions.

And it had to be printable and physical.

One folder, on one shelf, that a person having the worst week of their life could follow page by page while a cup of tea goes cold beside them.

I came across My Estate Kit through a thread on Gransnet.

A woman had posted photographs of her finished folder, and underneath them, the message her son sent after she showed him.

The comments were genuine.

Other women posting theirs, arguing about which pack to choose, the usual.

Their Family Handover Kit is built around exactly the shape Robert described.

They call it 5-28-6.

A Start Here card with the first actions in order.

A checklist for each stage.

A register for every account, pension and policy.

Ready to send letters for all the organisations Tell Us Once skips.

Written for England and Wales, in plain English, printed at home the same evening.

Every requirement I had written down, they had already addressed.

It was half past three in the morning.

The accounting had gone quiet.

I was sleeping through to six, the way I used to.

Jean noticed before David did.

She said I seemed lighter on our Tuesday walk, and I could not immediately explain why.

At the six week mark I ran my test again, because I could not wait any longer.

Sunday lunch.

I put the folder on the table in front of my youngest, Becky, and set her a challenge.

The boiler cover.

The deeds.

The life policy, and who it names.

I bought a pack of plastic wallets and rebuilt the Important box.

I typed our accounts into a spreadsheet.

I wrote the girls a letter about where everything was and put it in the bureau.

I told David, my husband, that everything was in the box, and he nodded the way husbands do.

Five months in, I ran a little test.

Sunday lunch, as casual as I could make it.

I asked David to find our buildings insurance and tell me when it renewed.

He found the box.

He found three statements from three different years and could not tell which was current.

He did not know which account the boiler cover came out of.

The password list was two years stale.

Twenty-five minutes in, he gave up and made a pot of tea.

Five months of genuine effort, and the box was still a scavenger hunt with a nicer label.

I was also noticing other things that bothered me.

The half past three accounting.

Lying awake, running through the list of what the girls would not know to look for.

The small jolt every time a renewal letter arrived from a company I had half forgotten we used.

I had always assumed that low hum was just part of being the organised one at 60.

It was not.

The shift for me came from an unexpected place.

A man named Robert H. gave a talk at a U3A meeting my neighbour Jean dragged me along to in October.

Retired probate practitioner.

Thirty-five years of it.

The talk was billed as "putting your affairs in order".

What it turned into was forty minutes on something I had never once heard explained properly.

He said the document families put their faith in, the will, is not the thing their children struggle with.

A will decides who inherits.

It does not tell anyone what exists, where it is kept, or the order in which nineteen different organisations need to hear the news, each with its own clock.

The struggle, he said, lives in the sequence.

And in England and Wales the sequence has a shape.

Five days.

The legal window to register, order enough certificates, locate the will, establish who is acting, arrange the farewell.

Roughly twenty-eight days.

The notifications.

Tell Us Once covers government departments and nothing else.

The bank, the mortgage, the insurers, the utilities, the private and workplace pensions, every one of those is a separate call, made in the right order or the wrong one.

Six months.

The deadline that catches everyone out.

Inheritance Tax is due by the end of the sixth month, and that clock does not pause while a family hunts for paperwork.

Then he said the thing that made me write a note in my phone.

"The families who cope are not the ones with the best wills.

They are the ones where somebody left a sequence to follow.

There is one thing I told my own children to expect from me, and it is not what any of you think it is."

Not a thicker will.

Not a safe.

Not an app.

A handover file, he said.

Built in the order of the actual process, not the order of a stationery catalogue.

The plan on top.

The records underneath, feeding it.

I went home and spent two evenings checking him against GOV.UK.

Not glossy websites.

The official pages.

He was right.

The five day registration window is real.

Tell Us Once really does stop at government departments.

The Inheritance Tax deadline really is the end of the sixth month.

It is all there, once you know to look.

So of course my first move was to order the cheapest thing on Amazon that looked the part.

A £12.99 journal with a linen cover, one of those "when I am gone" memory books.

I filled in about a third of it over six weeks.

Then I understood the mistake.

The chapters were alphabetical categories, not steps.

Half of it was American, with a page for social security and something called a 401k.

There was nowhere for the order of who to ring.

No deadlines.

No mention of probate or Tell Us Once anywhere in it.

I was essentially paying for nicer stationery.

It went in the drawer with the plastic wallets.

I went back to what Robert had actually described and wrote myself three requirements.

It had to be built on the real England and Wales sequence.

The registrar, Tell Us Once and everything it misses, probate, HMRC, the actual deadlines.

It had to hold the records that feed the plan.

Prompts for the exact reference numbers and documents each organisation asks for, not blank pages and good intentions.

And it had to be printable and physical.

One folder, on one shelf, that a person having the worst week of their life could follow page by page while a cup of tea goes cold beside them.

That is when I started looking at what was actually available to buy here.

I came across My Estate Kit through a thread on Gransnet.

A woman had posted photographs of her finished folder, and underneath them, the message her son sent after she showed him.

The comments were genuine.

Other women posting theirs, arguing about which pack to choose, the usual.

What sold me was their plan page.

Their Family Handover Kit is built around exactly the shape Robert described.

They call it 5-28-6.

A Start Here card with the first actions in order.

A checklist for each stage.

A register for every account, pension and policy.

Ready to send letters for all the organisations Tell Us Once skips.

Written for England and Wales, in plain English, printed at home the same evening.

Every requirement I had written down, they had already addressed.

👉 This is the kit, if you want to look while you read (from £29):

https://www.myestatekit.co.uk/v39-my-handover-kit

I ordered it on the Thursday.

I did not tell David.

I did not tell the girls.

I wanted to do it quietly, at my own pace, without anyone else's opinion in the room.

It took me two Sunday afternoons at the kitchen table.

The prompts tell you what goes where, so there was none of the blank page dread the journal gave me.

The first thing I noticed was not the folder.

It was half past three in the morning.

About nine days in, I realised I had stopped waking to run the list.

The accounting had gone quiet.

I was sleeping through to six, the way I used to.

Jean noticed before David did.

She said I seemed lighter on our Tuesday walk, and I could not immediately explain why.

At the six week mark I ran my test again, because I could not wait any longer.

Sunday lunch.

I put the folder on the table in front of my youngest, Becky, and set her a challenge.

The boiler cover.

Dad's workplace pension.

The deeds.

The life policy, and who it names.

Nineteen minutes.

No phone calls.

She found the lot, including two things I would have struggled to lay hands on a year earlier.

She went quiet at the end, which is not like her.

Then she said,

"Mum, this might be the kindest thing you have ever done for us."

Then April gave the folder a test I had not planned.

David had a fall and spent two nights in the Royal Shrewsbury.

In the flurry of it, I pulled his page and had his NHS number, his medications and his policy details at the front desk in under a minute, with my hands shaking.

That is when I understood the folder was never for some far off day.

It is for any Tuesday.

In May we had the wills looked over again, the scheduled visit.

I brought the folder along, mostly to ask where it ought to live.

I watched our solicitor leaf through it for a full two minutes.

He read the Start Here card twice.

Then he asked me where it was from, and wrote the name on his pad.

"I wish every client walked in with one of these," he said.

"Keep it with the will.

Not instead of it.

With it."

👉 This is what he was leafing through (from £29):

https://www.myestatekit.co.uk/v39-my-handover-kit

Here is what I would tell anyone my age who is sitting where I was sitting two years ago.

If you have made a will, well done, and keep it exactly where it is.

Robert was right about the two documents.

The will decides who inherits.

The folder is what your family will actually hold in their hands during the weeks the will cannot help them.

And if you decide to sort the folder, make sure it is actually the thing that works.

A memory journal with alphabetical chapters is not.

A spreadsheet only you understand is not.

A box of plastic wallets, I can tell you from experience, is not.

You want a plan built on the real England and Wales sequence, with the records that feed it, physical enough to sit on a shelf and be followed page by page by someone who has never done any of this before.

My Estate Kit is the only British kit I could find that meets all three straight off the page.

Theirs is the one with the 5-28-6 checklists, the account register and the letters for everyone Tell Us Once misses.

They offer a thirty day money back guarantee, which I think is fair, because thirty days is genuinely long enough to print it, fill it in and run the Sunday lunch test on your own family.

If it does not pass, you email them and that is that.

No forms, no argument.

The quiet in my head arrived inside the first fortnight.

The folder was done in two Sundays.

The proof came at six weeks, in nineteen minutes, over a roast chicken.

I am not telling anyone to skip the will or cancel the solicitor.

Ours drew ours up, and we will keep paying him to review it.

But if you are where I was, wills done, box file labelled, and that low hum at half past three you have learned to call normal, then the folder is the part nobody ever sat you down about.

I am still the one who holds this family together.

The difference is that now there is a version of me on paper who can do it on a day I cannot get to the phone.

I wish someone had told me at 58 what I know at 61.

I would have started earlier and skipped the worried years in between.

👉 If you want to look at it yourself, this is the one on my shelf (from £29):

https://www.myestatekit.co.uk/v39-my-handover-kit

body_text:
The Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia ran a study in 2018 on lottery winners. What they found was wild... 

For every $1,000 in lottery winnings someone in a neighbourhood won... the bankruptcy rate of their NEIGHBOURS went up by 2.4%.

Not the winners. The neighbours.

Let that sit for a second. Someone across the street wins money, and YOU are more likely to go broke. 

When you see someone nearby succeeding, you start making decisions based on what's working for them. New car. New kitchen. New wardrobe. New everything. Without realizing their context, their income, and their situation is completely different from yours.

It's "keeping up with the Joneses" but with receipts.

Phillip Jackson says this is exactly what happens to Shopify merchants every single day.

We see what Glossier is doing. We copy it.
We see what Gymshark is doing. We copy it.
We see what Ridge Wallet is doing. We copy it.
We see the Slack thread about what tech stack Kith uses. We copy it.

We read a Twitter thread about a $100M brand's email flow. We copy it.

And we do this WITHOUT asking...
...do their customers match mine?
...do their budgets match mine?
...does their stage match mine?
...does their margin structure match mine?
...does their audience give a crap about the same things?

usually no.

Here's my Shopify 1% takeaway for this one.
Next time you see a brand doing something cool and your first instinct is "we should do that"... pause.

Ask yourself three questions first:

Are their customers actually my customers?
Do I have the same margin structure to afford that move?
Am I copying the tactic or the thinking behind the tactic?

The tactic is usually the trap. The thinking is the gold.
Copy the thinking. Ignore the tactic. Run your own playbook.

🎧 Full episode link in bio, or: https://www.shopify1percent.com/futurecommerce/

body_text:
4 things every tracker on that list has in common — and the one thing Spotminders doesn't:

1. They all go silent in the cargo hold.
AirTag. Tile. Samsung. Ridge. Seven miles of air between your bag and the nearest relay. Not a glitch. Physics.

2. They all fail the 45-minute transfer window.
CDG. ORD. That's when bags get put on the wrong aircraft. That's the window every Bluetooth tracker cannot see.

3. They were all designed for something else.
Keys. Wallets. Coffee shops. Then repurposed for a cargo hold they were never built for.

4. None of them are in the pilot's own bag.
Spotminders is. Every deadhead flight. 60+ countries. Never flagged. Charged twice a year.

The passengers he's told don't refresh the airline app anymore. They walk straight to the belt.

Buy 3 Get 2 Free. Free wireless charger. Free shipping. Link below. 👇

body_text:
The first time I couldn't get up the ladder, I told my apprentice my back went out.

It hadn't.

I've torn off probably 800 roofs in my life and I know what a back going out feels like. It feels like someone shoved a knife between your spine and your kidney and twisted. This wasn't that. This was something else.

This was my knees forgetting they were knees.

My name is Greg. I'm 53. I'm a roofer in Fort Wayne, Indiana, and I've been on roofs since I was 17 years old. My dad was a roofer. His dad framed houses but did roofs in the summer to make extra money. I started Helton Roofing with my brother Dale in 1998 and we've been the guys you call in Allen County when a tree comes down on your garage or the shingles you put on in the 90s finally give up.

I'm telling you this because I want you to understand something before I tell you the rest of the story.

Roofing is not a job. It's a body. You don't roof for 36 years and have a body left over for other things. You spend your whole life giving pieces of yourself to other people's houses. Your knees go to the pitch. Your back goes to the bundles. Your shoulders go to the nail gun. Your hands go to the heat and the cold and the splinters and the cuts.

You know going in that you're trading.

You just don't know what the bill's going to look like when it comes due.

Mine came due on a Tuesday morning in May of last year, on a tear off in Aboite Township, on a ranch house with a 6/12 pitch and three layers of shingles that had to come off before lunch.

My apprentice that day was a kid named Tyler. 22 years old. Been with us about a year. Good kid, dumb in the way 22 year olds are dumb, hard worker, the kind of guy who'd jump off the truck and start tearing into something before I'd even finished telling him what we were doing.

We pulled up at 7:15. Tyler dropped the trailer. I went to set the ladder.

I want you to picture the ladder. 24 footer. Aluminum. The kind I've climbed maybe 40,000 times in my life. I could climb that ladder in my sleep. I have climbed it half asleep, hungover, with a fever, with a cut on my hand bleeding into my work glove, with my back so locked up I couldn't sit down.

I started up.

Rung one. Rung two. Rung three.

Rung four, my right knee made a noise I'd never heard come out of my body before.

It wasn't a pop. It wasn't a crack. It was kind of a wet sound. Like something inside the joint shifting around looking for a place to land.

And then my knee just stopped working.

Not painfully, exactly. It was worse than that. It just stopped responding. Like the wires between my brain and my leg got cut. I told my knee to bend. My knee did not bend. I told it again. Nothing.

I was four rungs up a ladder with my left foot on rung four and my right foot trying to get to rung five and not getting there.

I looked down. Tyler was at the bottom holding the ladder, staring up at me with a confused look on his face.

I said, "Come up here a second."

He climbed up behind me. I told him my back went out. I said I needed help getting down. He believed me because why wouldn't he. We got me down. I sat on the tailgate of the truck for 20 minutes. Tyler ran to the gas station and got me a Gatorade. I told him to call Dale and have him send another guy.

I drove home that afternoon with the worst feeling I have ever had in my life sitting in the seat next to me.

It wasn't pain.

It was a question.

The question was: Am I done?

I'm going to back up and tell you about the year before, because the ladder wasn't really the moment things broke. The ladder was the moment I had to admit they'd already broken.

Things had been going wrong for about 18 months.

It started in my hands. I'd be holding a nail gun and my fingers would just kind of seize up around the trigger. Not painfully. Just stuck. I'd have to put the gun down and shake my hand out for a minute and then go back to it. I figured it was the cold. We were in the middle of a January and I was pulling 10 hour days in 22 degree weather.

Then it was my shoulders. I'd be carrying a bundle of shingles up a ladder, 80 pounds on my shoulder, and halfway up I'd feel something in my rotator like a wet rope being pulled through a pipe. Not a tear. Something duller. I'd get to the top and have to set the bundle down and roll my shoulder for a minute before I could move.

Then it was my hips. I'd be sitting on the ridge of a roof drinking coffee on a break and when I went to stand up, my hips wouldn't unfold. Like they'd locked into the position I was sitting in. I'd have to grab the ridge with both hands and kind of pull myself up like an old man getting out of a recliner.

I was 52 years old.

52 is not old. My dad was working roofs at 67. My uncle Bert was on a ladder at 71. The guy who taught me how to swing a hammer, a man named Ralph who passed in 2011, was nailing down shingles at 74 and only stopped because his wife made him.

52 is not old in the roofing world.

But my body was acting like 70.

I went to my doctor. Dr. Reisman. He's been my doctor since the kids were in elementary school. Good guy. Late 50s. Plays golf. The kind of doctor who listens for about four minutes and then writes something down and tells you to lose weight.

I told him about my hands. My shoulders. My hips. My knees, which had started doing the thing where they'd ache for the first 20 minutes of every morning and then loosen up after I got moving.

He nodded. He moved my arms around. He pressed on my knees. He had me bend forward and touch my toes. I got down to my shins.

He sat back on his stool and said, "Greg, I'm going to be straight with you. You're 52 years old, you've been roofing since high school, and you're paying the bill. There's nothing structurally wrong here. This is wear and tear. This is what 36 years of roofs looks like."

I said, "What do I do about it?"

He said, "You can take ibuprofen for the pain. You can do some stretching. You can think about getting off the roof and into the office side of the business."

He said it like it was nothing. Like he was telling me to switch from a hardback to a softer chair.

Get off the roof.

I drove home that day in a kind of fog I'd never been in before. Get off the roof. The roof was where I lived. The roof was the only thing I'd ever been good at. My brother handles the books, the bidding, the customer calls. I do the work. I climb. I tear off. I lay down felt. I shingle. I'm the guy on the ladder.

Get off the roof was the same as saying get out of your own life.

I didn't tell my wife Patty. I didn't tell Dale. I just started taking the ibuprofen. Three in the morning. Three at lunch. Three before bed. Sometimes a fourth set when I got home if my knees were really yelling.

For about a month it helped. Took the edge off enough that I could keep moving.

Then it stopped helping. The pain came back through the medicine like water through a screen door.

So I doubled the dose. Six in the morning. Six at lunch. Six at night.

About six weeks into that, my stomach started bleeding. I didn't know that's what it was at first. I thought I had a stomach bug. Then the toilet bowl was black one morning and Patty saw it before I could flush.

We went to the ER. They told me I had two ulcers in my stomach. They told me to stop the ibuprofen immediately or I'd be on the operating table inside a year.

I stopped the ibuprofen.

The pain came roaring back inside 48 hours. Worse than before, somehow, like it had been waiting in the closet the whole time and now it was loose in the house.

That's when the ladder thing happened.

I'm sitting on the tailgate of my truck in Aboite Township that Tuesday morning, knee not working, Gatorade in my hand, and I'm doing math in my head.

The mortgage. The truck payment. Dale's kid is going to Purdue in the fall. Patty's been talking about retiring in five years. We've got a granddaughter, our daughter Megan's little girl Hailey, she's 4 years old and she calls me Pop and I am her favorite person on this earth.

How am I supposed to be Pop if I can't pick her up?

How am I supposed to take her fishing at Cedarville Reservoir like I told her I would, when I can't kneel down to bait the hook?

How am I supposed to walk her down the aisle if she ever gets that far, when I can barely walk to the mailbox without my knees burning?

I sat on that tailgate for 20 minutes and I felt every year of every roof come down on top of me at once.

Then I drove home.

I told Patty that night. The whole thing. The hands, the shoulders, the hips, the ladder, Reisman telling me to get off the roof. The ulcers. The math.

She didn't say anything for a long time. She got up and made me a sandwich and put it in front of me. Then she sat down across from me at the kitchen table and she said something that's stuck with me.

She said, "Greg, you need to stop trying to bandage this. You need to figure out what's actually going on inside you."

I didn't know what she meant. I don't think she knew what she meant either. But the sentence stuck.

Two weeks later, our neighbor Kenny came by to borrow the pressure washer.

Kenny is 56. Lives three houses down. He used to work at the GM plant in Roanoke before they shut it down. After the plant closed he started a small landscaping operation, mowing yards and doing fall cleanups for the neighborhood. He has hands like leather and a permanent farmer's tan and a Chevy with 230,000 miles on it.

I was on the porch when he came up the driveway. I was sitting because standing too long made my hips lock. He came up the steps and stopped on the second one and looked at me.

He said, "You look terrible."

I said, "Thanks, Kenny."

He sat down on the step. He said, "What's going on with you?"

So I told him. Most of it. Not the part about Hailey. The rest of it.

Kenny listened. He pulled a piece of dried grass out of his pant cuff and rolled it between his fingers while he listened.

When I was done he said, "Greg. You remember the year I couldn't get out of my truck?"

I did remember. About four years ago Kenny had a stretch of about eight months where he was in real bad shape. Knees. Shoulders. Back. He'd be sitting in his truck at the end of a job and his wife would have to come out to the driveway to help him get the door open and his legs out.

I'd forgotten about it because Kenny had been fine for years now. Mowing his yards. Climbing in and out of the truck like a 30 year old.

I said, "Yeah. What happened? You ever figure that out?"

He looked at me and said, "My wife's sister sent me something. From India, originally. Some kind of berry."

I almost laughed. A berry. I'm sitting there with two ulcers and knees that won't bend and Kenny is telling me about a berry.

He saw the look on my face. He said, "Greg. I'm telling you. I was where you are. I was about to sell the truck and the mower and the trailer. I was looking at signing up for a desk job at the Lowe's in Jefferson Pointe. My wife's sister, Linda, she lives outside of Indianapolis, she'd been on this stuff for about a year for her own joint problems and she sent me a bottle. Said try it for two months. If nothing changes, throw it out."

I said, "And?"

He said, "Eight weeks in, I was back in the truck. Twelve weeks in, I was mowing again. I've been on it three and a half years now. I'm 56 years old and I climbed a 12 foot ladder yesterday to clean Mrs. Henderson's gutters and my knees didn't say a word."

He told me what it was. Amla. Spelled it out for me. Said it was Indian gooseberry, said the same berry had been used in traditional medicine for thousands of years, said his sister in law had told him it was one of the most studied fruits in the world that nobody in America has ever heard of.

He said the brand he took was called Auniva. Said his sister in law had switched to it because the bottle was sourced and tested in the U.S. and the company had a money back guarantee.

He left the pressure washer cleaner than I expected and he walked back down the driveway and I sat on the porch for another hour thinking.

That night I got on my laptop after Patty went to bed.

I'm going to tell you what I learned because nobody at Reisman's office ever explained any of this to me, and I think for guys like me, guys who've been told it's wear and tear and aging and there's nothing structural wrong, this stuff matters.

The thing they don't tell you about joint pain is that the joint isn't the whole story.

The joint is where you feel the pain. But what's causing the pain is mostly happening at a level you can't see, in the cells that surround the joint and the tissues that connect the joint to everything else.

There are two big drivers.

The first is inflammation. Not the kind of inflammation you see when you sprain your ankle and it puffs up. The other kind. The quiet, chronic kind that lives in your tissues for years and slowly grinds you down. Inflammatory signals running through your body all day every day, irritating cartilage, irritating tendons, irritating the lining of the joint capsule itself. You can't feel it directly. But you feel its effects. Stiffness in the morning. Aches that don't quit. Joints that lock up after you sit too long. Hands that won't unclench.

The second is oxidative stress. The fancy way of saying your cells are getting rusted. Free radicals are produced naturally by your body, but as you age, especially if you've been hard on your body for decades, the rate of damage outruns the rate of repair. Cartilage cells take the hit. Tendon cells take the hit. The synovial fluid that's supposed to lubricate the joint thins out. The whole system starts running rough.

What ibuprofen does is shut down one inflammatory pathway. It works in the short term. But it doesn't do anything about the oxidative damage. And it tears holes in your stomach lining as the price of admission, which is how I ended up with two ulcers.

Amla is interesting because it works on both sides of the problem.

It's been studied for a long time as one of the most concentrated natural sources of antioxidants on earth. Loaded with vitamin C, polyphenols, tannins. The kind of compounds that have been linked to quieting oxidative stress at the cellular level.

It's also been associated with supporting a healthy inflammatory response in the body. Not by shutting down inflammation entirely, which is what ibuprofen does. By helping the body's own systems regulate the inflammatory signaling more naturally.

What that translates to in plain English is that Amla has been linked to supporting joint comfort, supporting connective tissue, and supporting the cellular environment that keeps your knees bending and your hands gripping and your shoulders moving.

I read about it for three nights straight. Down the rabbit hole. Studies from India. Studies from Europe. Reviews in mainstream medical journals.

The information was just sitting there. Nobody had ever told me about it.

Not Reisman. Not the ER doctor who told me to stop the ibuprofen. Not a single person in 36 years of working a body to the bone.

I ordered a bottle of Auniva Amla on a Friday night. It came the following Wednesday.

Two capsules with breakfast. That's it.

The first two weeks I was honestly waiting for nothing to happen. I'd been let down by enough things at that point that I was already planning on returning the bottle.

Week three, something changed in my hands. I noticed it on a Monday morning, getting dressed. Buttoning my shirt. The buttons used to be a small daily fight. That morning I just buttoned my shirt and walked out of the bedroom. I didn't realize I'd done it until I was halfway through breakfast.

I told Patty. She said, "Don't jinx it."

Week five, the morning stiffness in my knees got shorter. Used to be 20 minutes of walking it off before I felt human. Then it was 15. Then it was 10.

Week seven, I climbed a ladder.

I want to tell you about that ladder because it's the moment my life pivoted.

It was a small job. A neighbor down the street, Mrs. Cordova, asked me to look at a leak around her chimney. I told Patty I was just going to look. I drove over with Tyler. I was honestly going to climb up two rungs, take a picture with my phone, and come back down.

I went up two rungs. Then four. Then six.

Then I was on the roof.

I walked the perimeter. I crouched down at the chimney flashing. I crouched down. My knees bent. They bent without complaining. They bent like I was 35 years old.

I sat down on the ridge of Mrs. Cordova's roof and I looked out over the neighborhood and I cried.

Tyler was at the bottom of the ladder. He didn't see me. I'm glad.

I came down the ladder one rung at a time, slow, the way I'd been coming down ladders for two years, but my knees weren't yelling. My hips weren't locking. My shoulders weren't burning. I came down a ladder like a man.

That was nine months ago.

I'm still on the roof.

I picked up Hailey at her preschool last Thursday. She runs at me when I come into the lobby and I scoop her up and put her on my hip and walk out to the truck. I haven't done that in three years. Megan watched me do it and she got quiet in the kind of way mothers get quiet when something they didn't think would happen happens.

Patty asked me on Sunday if I was thinking about retiring early.

I said, "Patty, I just got back to work."

I want to say one more thing.

There's a particular kind of feeling that comes with being a man who works with his hands and starts losing them. It's not just the pain. It's the identity. You spend your whole life being the guy who can fix it, lift it, climb it, carry it. And then one day you're standing four rungs up a ladder and your knee won't bend and you realize you're becoming somebody you don't recognize. Somebody who needs help. Somebody who watches.

That's worse than the pain.

I lost about 18 months to that feeling. I don't get those months back. I don't get the day Hailey wanted me to lift her up onto the kitchen counter to help bake cookies and I had to tell her Pop's back hurt. I don't get the day my brother had to take a job I should have been on because I couldn't climb the ladder.

But I get the rest.

And if you're a roofer or a plumber or a mechanic or a framer or anybody whose body is the tool you use to feed your family, and your knees are starting to talk to you in the morning, and your hands are starting to seize up, and your doctor is telling you it's wear and tear and to think about a desk job, I want you to know there's another way to think about this.

The pain in your joints isn't the whole story. The story is the inflammation and the oxidation that's been quietly running through your body for years while you were giving everything you had to other people's houses.

Auniva Amla supports the system that's supposed to keep that under control. Two capsules a day. 90 day money back guarantee. If your body doesn't tell you something is different inside two months, you send the bottle back and you don't pay a dime.

Kenny told me to try it for two months. I'm telling you the same thing.

You traded a lot for the work you do.

It doesn't have to be the trade you thought it was.

P.S. Tyler is on the roof beside me again. He never asked me what really happened that day in Aboite Township. I think he knew. He's a good kid. I told him on a roof in Huntington a couple weeks ago, both of us sitting on the ridge eating a sandwich, what had actually been going on. I told him about the berry. He laughed. Then he stopped laughing. He told me his dad, who's a millwright in Decatur, has been having the same kind of year I had. Hands. Shoulders. Hips. He asked me to write the name down for him. I wrote it on the back of a Helton Roofing card and he put it in his wallet. He texted me last week. His dad's been on it three weeks. His dad walked the dog Saturday morning for the first time since November.

P.P.S. The 90 day money back guarantee is what got me to try it and it's what I want you to think about. When Reisman told me to take ibuprofen and the ibuprofen tore holes in my stomach, nobody offered me a refund on the ulcers. When I lost 18 months of work to a body that quit on me, nobody offered me a refund on the months. The supplement aisle at Walgreens doesn't offer refunds. Doctors don't offer refunds. The only people I've ever found who offer to refund a thing that doesn't work are the people who actually believe in what they're selling. Try it for two months. If it doesn't move the needle, send it back. You're risking nothing. I risked 18 months. Don't do that.

P.P.P.S. If you're a tradesman and you've been quietly thinking about getting off the tools, if you've been telling your wife your back is fine when it isn't, if you've been letting the younger guy on the crew do the work you used to do, if you've been sitting in the truck at the end of the day for an extra ten minutes before you can stand up, this is what I want to tell you. You traded your body for your work. You don't get to undo the trade. But you might be able to renegotiate it. Two capsules. A glass of water. A small green berry from a tree on the other side of the world. 36 years of roofs. A 4 year old granddaughter who calls me Pop. A ladder I climbed last Thursday on a tear off in New Haven, all the way up, no help, no story to tell my apprentice. That's the renegotiation. That's what's available.

I told Patty. She said, "Don't jinx it."

Week five, the morning stiffness in my knees got shorter. Used to be 20 minutes of walking it off before I felt human. Then it was 15. Then it was 10.

I went up two rungs. Then four. Then six.

Then I was on the roof.

I walked the perimeter. I crouched down at the chimney flashing. I crouched down. My knees bent. They bent without complaining. They bent like I was 35 years old.

I sat down on the ridge of Mrs. Cordova's roof and I looked out over the neighborhood and I cried.

The first time I couldn't get up the ladder, I told my apprentice my back went out.

It hadn't.

I've torn off probably 800 roofs in my life and I know what a back going out feels like. It feels like someone shoved a knife between your spine and your kidney and twisted. This wasn't that. This was something else.

This was my knees forgetting they were knees.

My name is Greg. I'm 53. I'm a roofer in Fort Wayne, Indiana, and I've been on roofs since I was 17 years old. My dad was a roofer. His dad framed houses but did roofs in the summer to make extra money. I started Helton Roofing with my brother Dale in 1998 and we've been the guys you call in Allen County when a tree comes down on your garage or the shingles you put on in the 90s finally give up.

I'm telling you this because I want you to understand something before I tell you the rest of the story.

Roofing is not a job. It's a body. You don't roof for 36 years and have a body left over for other things. You spend your whole life giving pieces of yourself to other people's houses. Your knees go to the pitch. Your back goes to the bundles. Your shoulders go to the nail gun. Your hands go to the heat and the cold and the splinters and the cuts.

You know going in that you're trading.

You just don't know what the bill's going to look like when it comes due.

Mine came due on a Tuesday morning in May of last year, on a tear off in Aboite Township, on a ranch house with a 6/12 pitch and three layers of shingles that had to come off before lunch.

My apprentice that day was a kid named Tyler. 22 years old. Been with us about a year. Good kid, dumb in the way 22 year olds are dumb, hard worker, the kind of guy who'd jump off the truck and start tearing into something before I'd even finished telling him what we were doing.

We pulled up at 7:15. Tyler dropped the trailer. I went to set the ladder.

I want you to picture the ladder. 24 footer. Aluminum. The kind I've climbed maybe 40,000 times in my life. I could climb that ladder in my sleep. I have climbed it half asleep, hungover, with a fever, with a cut on my hand bleeding into my work glove, with my back so locked up I couldn't sit down.

I started up.

Rung one. Rung two. Rung three.

Rung four, my right knee made a noise I'd never heard come out of my body before.

It wasn't a pop. It wasn't a crack. It was kind of a wet sound. Like something inside the joint shifting around looking for a place to land.

And then my knee just stopped working.

Not painfully, exactly. It was worse than that. It just stopped responding. Like the wires between my brain and my leg got cut. I told my knee to bend. My knee did not bend. I told it again. Nothing.

I was four rungs up a ladder with my left foot on rung four and my right foot trying to get to rung five and not getting there.

I looked down. Tyler was at the bottom holding the ladder, staring up at me with a confused look on his face.

I said, "Come up here a second."

He climbed up behind me. I told him my back went out. I said I needed help getting down. He believed me because why wouldn't he. We got me down. I sat on the tailgate of the truck for 20 minutes. Tyler ran to the gas station and got me a Gatorade. I told him to call Dale and have him send another guy.

I drove home that afternoon with the worst feeling I have ever had in my life sitting in the seat next to me.

It wasn't pain.

It was a question.

The question was: Am I done?

I'm going to back up and tell you about the year before, because the ladder wasn't really the moment things broke. The ladder was the moment I had to admit they'd already broken.

Things had been going wrong for about 18 months.

It started in my hands. I'd be holding a nail gun and my fingers would just kind of seize up around the trigger. Not painfully. Just stuck. I'd have to put the gun down and shake my hand out for a minute and then go back to it. I figured it was the cold. We were in the middle of a January and I was pulling 10 hour days in 22 degree weather.

Then it was my shoulders. I'd be carrying a bundle of shingles up a ladder, 80 pounds on my shoulder, and halfway up I'd feel something in my rotator like a wet rope being pulled through a pipe. Not a tear. Something duller. I'd get to the top and have to set the bundle down and roll my shoulder for a minute before I could move.

Then it was my hips. I'd be sitting on the ridge of a roof drinking coffee on a break and when I went to stand up, my hips wouldn't unfold. Like they'd locked into the position I was sitting in. I'd have to grab the ridge with both hands and kind of pull myself up like an old man getting out of a recliner.

I was 52 years old.

52 is not old. My dad was working roofs at 67. My uncle Bert was on a ladder at 71. The guy who taught me how to swing a hammer, a man named Ralph who passed in 2011, was nailing down shingles at 74 and only stopped because his wife made him.

52 is not old in the roofing world.

But my body was acting like 70.

I went to my doctor. Dr. Reisman. He's been my doctor since the kids were in elementary school. Good guy. Late 50s. Plays golf. The kind of doctor who listens for about four minutes and then writes something down and tells you to lose weight.

I told him about my hands. My shoulders. My hips. My knees, which had started doing the thing where they'd ache for the first 20 minutes of every morning and then loosen up after I got moving.

He nodded. He moved my arms around. He pressed on my knees. He had me bend forward and touch my toes. I got down to my shins.

He sat back on his stool and said, "Greg, I'm going to be straight with you. You're 52 years old, you've been roofing since high school, and you're paying the bill. There's nothing structurally wrong here. This is wear and tear. This is what 36 years of roofs looks like."

I said, "What do I do about it?"

He said, "You can take ibuprofen for the pain. You can do some stretching. You can think about getting off the roof and into the office side of the business."

He said it like it was nothing. Like he was telling me to switch from a hardback to a softer chair.

Get off the roof.

I drove home that day in a kind of fog I'd never been in before. Get off the roof. The roof was where I lived. The roof was the only thing I'd ever been good at. My brother handles the books, the bidding, the customer calls. I do the work. I climb. I tear off. I lay down felt. I shingle. I'm the guy on the ladder.

Get off the roof was the same as saying get out of your own life.

I didn't tell my wife Patty. I didn't tell Dale. I just started taking the ibuprofen. Three in the morning. Three at lunch. Three before bed. Sometimes a fourth set when I got home if my knees were really yelling.

For about a month it helped. Took the edge off enough that I could keep moving.

Then it stopped helping. The pain came back through the medicine like water through a screen door.

So I doubled the dose. Six in the morning. Six at lunch. Six at night.

About six weeks into that, my stomach started bleeding. I didn't know that's what it was at first. I thought I had a stomach bug. Then the toilet bowl was black one morning and Patty saw it before I could flush.

We went to the ER. They told me I had two ulcers in my stomach. They told me to stop the ibuprofen immediately or I'd be on the operating table inside a year.

I stopped the ibuprofen.

The pain came roaring back inside 48 hours. Worse than before, somehow, like it had been waiting in the closet the whole time and now it was loose in the house.

That's when the ladder thing happened.

The mortgage. The truck payment. Dale's kid is going to Purdue in the fall. Patty's been talking about retiring in five years. We've got a granddaughter, our daughter Megan's little girl Hailey, she's 4 years old and she calls me Pop and I am her favorite person on this earth.

I sat on that tailgate for 20 minutes and I felt every year of every roof come down on top of me at once.

Then I drove home.

I told Patty that night. The whole thing. The hands, the shoulders, the hips, the ladder, Reisman telling me to get off the roof. The ulcers. The math.

I didn't know what she meant. I don't think she knew what she meant either. But the sentence stuck.

I said, "Yeah. What happened? You ever figure that out?"

He looked at me and said, "My wife's sister sent me something. From India, originally. Some kind of berry."

The thing they don't tell you about joint pain is that the joint isn't the whole story.

The joint is where you feel the pain. But what's causing the pain is mostly happening at a level you can't see, in the cells that surround the joint and the tissues that connect the joint to everything else.

There are two big drivers.

The first is inflammation. Not the kind of inflammation you see when you sprain your ankle and it puffs up. The other kind.
